mool: There is one God, Ik Oankar, the One who pervades all and is ever the same; his Name is Sat (the One who truly is); he is the Creator, the Being who dwells in all, without fear, without enmity, his form beyond time, unborn, self-existent, realised by the Guru's grace.
These four lines are the Mool Mantar (the root statement), which stands at the head of the Guru Granth Sahib; the bani (sacred composition) Jap begins after it.

ੴ is the numeral ੧ joined to the letter ਓ with an open stroke above it, read Ik Oankar: the numeral says that God is one, without a second, and the stroke (kaar) that the One is ever the same and pervades all.
Sat (Sanskrit satya, from the root as, to be) means the One who truly exists, always; ਨਾਮੁ with the aunkar is the subject: his Name is Sat.
Purakh in Gurbani is the Being who pervades the whole creation, not a man.

In Akaal Moorat, moorat (with sihari) is a feminine noun, form, and akaal agrees with it: a form that time and death do not touch. It is a different word from moorat with the aunkar (ਮੂਰਤੁ, Sanskrit muhūrta), a moment of time.
Ajooni: not born into any of the forms of life. Saibhang (Sanskrit svayambhū): existing of himself, made by no one.
jap: Jap: the bani to be recited with the mind on God.
ਜਪੁ (with the aunkar) is a noun, the name of the whole bani that follows; it is called Japji Sahib out of reverence.
salok.open: The True One was there in the beginning; the True One was there when the ages began. The True One exists now as well, O Nanak, and the True One will be hereafter too. ॥1॥
Sach (Sanskrit satya, from as, to be) is here God himself, the One who truly and always exists; the salok names every time: before all things, at the start of the ages, now, and hereafter.
p1: Purity (of mind) does not come from washing (the body), though I wash a hundred thousand times. Silence (of mind) does not come from keeping silent, though I stay absorbed in an unbroken thread of attention. While I live in craving, the hunger does not go, though I tie up the loads (of goods) of all the worlds. Though I had thousands, even hundreds of thousands, of clever ways, not one would go along with me. How, then, can one become Sachiar (one who is true), and how is the wall of falsehood to be broken? O Nanak, by walking in the Hukam (God's order, his will) of the Lord whose will it is; this (way) is written along with (every being from the start). ॥1॥

Soch here is ritual washing and the purity it is meant to bring (Sanskrit śauca), not thought: the first four lines take the mind's purity, silence, hunger and cleverness in turn, and cleverness of thought is line 4. The line is also read as: by thinking, he cannot be conceived.
Liv taar: an unbroken thread of attention, the long, fixed trance of the ascetic.
The puris are the worlds (of the gods and men); their loads are all the goods they hold.
Sachiar (sach + alaya, an abode of truth) is one in whom the True One can shine. Line 5 asks the question that the whole Japji answers.
The wall of falsehood is the wall that stands between the soul and God.

Hukam is the order by which God makes and runs all things; Rajaai is the Lord whose raza (will) it is. ਹੁਕਮਿ with the sihari means in the Hukam; what is written along with every being from the beginning is this walking (ਚਲਣਾ) in the Hukam. It is also read as: the Hukam is written along with each being.
p2: By the Hukam, forms come into being; the Hukam cannot be described. By the Hukam, beings come into being; by the Hukam, glory is received. By the Hukam, one is high and another low; by the Hukam, as it is written, sorrows and joys are received. Some, by the Hukam, are blessed with grace; others, by the Hukam, are made to wander forever (through births and deaths). Everyone is within the Hukam; no one is outside the Hukam. O Nanak, if one understands the Hukam, then no one speaks in Haumai (ego). ॥2॥
The pauri does not say what the Hukam is, since it cannot be told (line 1); it says what the Hukam does: it makes every form and every being and gives each its lot.
Bhavaaeeah (causative passive): they are made to wander, through birth after birth.
Haumai, literally I-I, is the sense of a separate self that says I did this, I will do that; one who sees that everything moves by the Hukam no longer speaks so.
p3: Someone sings of his might, if anyone has the might (to sing it). Someone sings of his gifts, taking them as his sign. Someone sings of his virtues and his beautiful glories. Someone sings, through learning, of hard thought about him. Someone sings that he makes the body and then turns it to dust. Someone sings that he takes away lives and gives them again. Someone sings that he seems far off, that he appears far away. Someone sings that he watches (all), ever present, face to face. The telling (of him) never runs short. Millions upon millions have told of him, telling and telling again. The Giver goes on giving, and those who take from him grow tired. Through age after age, they go on eating (what he gives). The Commander's Hukam drives the way (of the world). O Nanak, the carefree (Lord) is ever in bloom. ॥3॥
Each singer praises the side of God he has seen: power, gifts, virtues, learned philosophy, the making and unmaking of bodies, distance, nearness. Lines 9 and 10 say that no telling reaches the end.
Chaar is the adjective beautiful (Sanskrit cāru); the number four is chaar with a sihari (ਚਾਰਿ). Some read it as four, the four Vedas.
Haadraa hadoor (Arabic haazir, present; huzoor, presence): present and in sight, face to face.
Hukami in line 13 is God himself, the one whose Hukam it is.
Veparvaah, free of care: giving to all, through all the ages, never burdens him.
p4: The Master is true, and true is his justice; his language is love, and he is without limit. All of us ask and beg him to give and give, and the Giver bestows his gifts. What, then, should we place before him, by which his court may be seen? What words should we speak with our mouth, on hearing which he may give us his love? In the Amrit vela (the hours of nectar before daybreak), (remember) the true Naam (the Name, God's presence remembered) and reflect on his greatness. By his grace comes the robe (of honour); by his glance of grace, the door of liberation. O Nanak, in this way it is known that the True One himself is everywhere. ॥4॥

Naai is read as niaai, justice, the law by which he runs the world: the subject form ਸਾਚੁ needs a subject noun, and the Name as subject is ਨਾਉ, as in line 5. The words are also read as: true is his Name.
His language is love: love is the speech in which he is reached and in which he speaks to us.
Lines 3 and 4 ask what offering and what words could win him, since every gift is already his; lines 5 to 7 give the answer.
Amrit vela: the last watch of the night before dawn, when the mind is free of the day's affairs.

Karam is grace (Arabic-Persian karam), as in Pauri 6 and Pauri 24. The robe is the robe of honour a king bestows, here the gift of his praise and love. Others read karam as one's past deeds and the robe as the body of this human birth.
Sachiar here is God, the home of all truth; in Pauri 1 the word is the person made fit for the True One.
p5: He cannot be installed, nor can he be made. That stainless one, Niranjan, exists of himself alone. Whoever has served him has won honour. O Nanak, let us sing of him, the treasure of virtues. Let us sing, let us listen, and keep love for him in the mind. Whoever does so casts off sorrow and carries peace home. Through the Guru comes the Naad, through the Guru comes the Veda; through the Guru, God is known to pervade all. The Guru is Shiva, the Guru is Gorakh and Brahma, the Guru is mother Parvati. Even if I come to know him, I cannot tell of him; he cannot be put into words. O Guru, give me this one understanding: all beings have one giver; may I never forget him. ॥5॥
Thapia is to set up and install, as an image is installed and consecrated in a temple; kita is made or fashioned. God is neither installed by anyone nor fashioned by anyone.
Niranjan is nir, without, and anjan, collyrium, the black of eye-paint: the one on whom Maya (the world's illusion and lure) leaves no stain.
To serve God here is to remember him and worship him.
Gaviai, suniai and rakhiai are a gentle call to all, let us sing, let us listen, let us keep; the call runs from line 4 into line 5.
Ghari, home, is the heart: peace comes to dwell within.

Gurmukhi here means through the Guru. The Naad is the sacred sound the yogis meditate on (and the horn they blow), the Veda the Brahmins' scripture; here they stand for the Shabad (the Word, the Naam) and true knowledge, both of which come through the Guru. It is also read: the Guru's word is the Naad, the Guru's word is the Veda.

Isar (Ishvar) is Shiva. Gorakh, keeper of the earth (go, earth; rakh, keeper), is read as Vishnu, the sustainer; some take him to be Gorakhnath, master of the Nath yogis. Parvati is Shiva's consort; the Faridkot Teeka takes mai to include Lakshmi and Saraswati. The line says the Guru is, for the disciple, all the gods and goddesses that others worship.
Je hau jana is read: even if I come to know him, I cannot describe him. It is also read as a question: if I knew him, would I not tell? Either way, he is beyond words.
In gura ik dehi bujhai, ik has no aunkar: it is feminine, going with bujhai, understanding. In iku data, iku has aunkar: masculine, going with data, the one Giver.
p6: I would bathe at a tirath (a place of pilgrimage) if by that I pleased him; without pleasing him, what would I gain by bathing? All the creation he has brought forth that I see: without his grace, what does anyone receive, what can anyone take? Jewels, gems and rubies lie within one's own understanding, if one listens to a single teaching of the Guru. O Guru, give me this one understanding: all beings have one giver; may I never forget him. ॥6॥
Bathing at a tirath, on a river or a sacred pool, is held to wash away sin.
Nava, bhava and vekha end in the first person: I bathe, I please, I see. Nai is having bathed.
Karam here is grace, the Arabic-Persian karam, as in Pauri 4; it is also read as good deeds, karma.
The jewels, gems and rubies are the precious virtues that the Guru's teaching wakes in the mind.
p7: Even if a person's life spanned the four ages, or ten times more, if they were known throughout the nine regions of the earth, and everyone walked with them, if, having made a good name, they won praise and renown in the world, yet if they do not come into his gracious sight, no one asks after them. God makes such a one a worm among worms, holds them guilty and lays the blame on them. O Nanak, God creates virtue in the virtueless, and gives virtue to the virtuous. No one else like him comes to mind who could give the virtueless one any virtue. ॥7॥
The four ages (yugas) are Satyug, Treta, Duapar and Kalyug, together 4,320,000 years in the Puranic reckoning.
The nine khands are the nine regions into which Puranic geography divides the earth: the whole world.
Nadar is God's glance of grace, from the Persian nazar.
Kari, having made, is a conjunct participle, so the one who makes them a worm is also the one who lays the blame: God. It is also read: even sinners lay blame on them.
Nirguni, with sihari, is locative: God creates virtue in the virtueless. Gunvantia is plural: to the virtuous.
Tisu here is the virtueless one of the line before: none but God can give that one virtue. It is also read: no one can do God any good in return.
p8: By listening, one rises to the station of the Siddhas, the Pirs, the gods and the Naths. By listening, one comes to understand the earth, the bull Dhaul said to bear it, and the sky. By listening, one comes to understand the continents, the worlds and the nether regions. By listening, death cannot touch one. O Nanak, the devotees are ever in bloom. By listening, sorrow and sin are destroyed. ॥8॥
Suniai is by listening: listening to the Lord's praise with the attention fixed on the Naam. Pauris 8 to 11 tell what listening brings; Pauris 12 to 15 go on to accepting (mannai).

The first line has no verb. We read it as what listening brings: the one who listens rises to the station of the Siddhas, Pirs, gods and Naths. The Faridkot Teeka reads: they won their station by listening.
Siddhas are yogis held to have perfected their practice and won powers; Pirs are Muslim spiritual guides; Naths are the masters of Gorakh's order of yogis. Suri are the gods.
Dhaul (dhaval, white) is the bull of legend that bears the earth on its horns; Pauri 16 names dharam as the true bull. Listening opens the understanding of the earth, what holds it up, and the sky.
Dip are the seven continents (dvipas) of Puranic geography, loa the worlds (lokas) above, and patal the nether regions below.
Kaal is death, and time that brings it; its fear cannot touch the one who listens.
Bhagta is plural, the devotees. Vigasu is blossoming, as a lotus opens: a joy that does not fade.
p9: By listening, one rises to the station of Shiva, Brahma and Indra. By listening, even a wicked person utters the Lord's praises with his mouth. By listening, one comes to know the way of yoga and the secrets of the body. By listening, one comes to understand the Shastras, the Simritis and the Vedas. O Nanak, the devotees are ever in bloom. By listening, sorrow and sin are destroyed. ॥9॥
Brahma is the creator and Indra the king of the gods. As in Pauri 8, listening raises one to the station they are honoured for.
Salahan is a noun, praises, and mandu is singular, a wicked person: the wicked man himself sings the Lord's praises. The line is also read: the wicked come to be praised; but salahan is not a verb.
Jog jugat is the way of yoga, union with God; tan bhed, the secrets of the body, are the hidden workings of the body and its senses.
The Shastras are the Hindu treatises of philosophy, the Simritis the codes of law and custom, and the Vedas the oldest scriptures.
p10: By listening come generosity, contentment and knowledge of God. By listening, one has the bath at the sixty-eight tiraths. By listening, one receives the honour that scholars win by reading and reading. By listening, the mind's attention settles in Sahaj (natural, unshaken poise). O Nanak, the devotees are ever in bloom. By listening, sorrow and sin are destroyed. ॥10॥

Satu, with aunkar, is read as generosity, giving: the virtue Gurbani pairs with contentment, as in satia mani santokhu upjai dene kai vichari (Asa di Var), where the sati are the givers. Many read it as truth.
The sixty-eight tiraths are the chief Hindu places of pilgrimage; listening is, as it were, a bath at them all.
Pari pari pavahi manu: those who read and read win honour. The line says that this honour comes by listening.
Sahaj (saha, with; ja, born) is the state natural to the soul: steady, beyond the pull of Maya's three qualities. Sahaji, with sihari, is locative: in Sahaj.
p11: By listening, one comes to fathom oceans of virtue. By listening, one rises to the station of the Sheikhs, the Pirs and the kings. By listening, the blind find the way. By listening, the depth of the fathomless ocean is found. O Nanak, the devotees are ever in bloom. By listening, sorrow and sin are destroyed. ॥11॥
Sara guna ke: of the oceans (literally pools) of virtues; gah, those who wade in and fathom them.
Sheikhs are Muslim religious leaders; as with the Pirs in Pauri 8, listening raises one to their station.
The blind are those without understanding; the way is the way to God.

Hath here is feminine: the depth that can be sounded, a footing. Asgahu is the fathomless ocean, the world, whose depth listening lets one measure. It is also read: the unfathomable Lord becomes as plain as a thing in one's hand.
p12: The state of one who has accepted (the Naam) cannot be told. If anyone tries to tell it, he regrets it afterwards. There is no one to write it on paper with a pen; people sit together and reflect on the one who has accepted. So exalted is the immaculate Naam (of God); (this is known) if someone accepts it and comes to know it in his own mind. ॥12॥
Pauris 12 to 15 follow the four pauris of listening: to accept (mannana) is to take the Naam into a convinced mind, to trust it and live by it, the step that comes after hearing it.
In this pauri manne, followed by ki and ka, means of one who has accepted; in Pauris 13 to 15 mannai means by accepting, as suniai in Pauris 8 to 11 means by listening.

Niranjan (nir, without, and anjan, the black of collyrium) means stainless, untouched by Maya. It has the same ending as Naam beside it, so it describes the Naam itself. These last two lines close each of Pauris 12 to 15.
p13: By accepting (the Naam), awareness and understanding arise in the mind. By accepting, one comes to know of all the worlds. By accepting, one does not suffer blows on the face. By accepting, one does not go with Jam (the messenger of Death). So exalted is the immaculate Naam (of God); (this is known) if someone accepts it and comes to know it in his own mind. ॥13॥
Surat is the mind's awareness and attention; sudh, in the next line, is knowing, insight.
Blows on the face are an image of punishment and disgrace. Prof. Sahib Singh takes them as the blows of the vices, the Faridkot Teeka as the blows of Jam.
Jam (Yama) is Death and his messengers, who in Indian belief lead the soul away for judgement; to go with Jam is to be caught in death and rebirth.
p14: By accepting (the Naam), no obstacle blocks one's way. By accepting, one departs (from the world) with honour, known to all. By accepting, one does not walk the many roads and paths (of the sects). By accepting, one's bond is with dharam (righteousness). So exalted is the immaculate Naam (of God); (this is known) if someone accepts it and comes to know it in his own mind. ॥14॥
Pargat is openly known: one who accepts leaves the world honoured and in good name.
Mag and panth are two words for a road; here they are the many separate ways of the sects. One who accepts is joined to dharam directly and is not pulled from one way to another.
Dharam here is righteousness, the true way of life, not a creed.
p15: By accepting (the Naam), people find the door of liberation. By accepting, one gives his family, too, (God's) support. By accepting, the Guru himself crosses over and carries the Sikhs across. By accepting, O Nanak, they do not wander about begging. So exalted is the immaculate Naam (of God); (this is known) if someone accepts it and comes to know it in his own mind. ॥15॥
Sadhar is sa-adhar, with a support: one who accepts makes his family, too, lean on God.

Guru, with the ending -u, is the subject; Sikh, without it, is plural, the ones carried across. Another reading takes the one who accepts as the subject: he crosses over and, as a guru, carries his Sikhs across.
They do not wander begging: they are not dependent on one door after another. The Faridkot Teeka reads bhikh as the beggar's round through the countless births.
p16: The Panch (those who have listened and accepted the Naam) are approved, the Panch are foremost. It is the Panch who receive honour in the Dargah (the Lord's court). It is the Panch who shine at the courts of kings. The Panch keep their attention on the one Guru alone. If anyone speaks of (the creation) and reflects on it, (even then) there is no counting the Creator's making. The bull (that holds up the earth) is dharam, the son of compassion, which in its order has firmly established contentment. If anyone understands this, he becomes Sachiar. How great a load is on the bull! Beneath the earth there would be another (bull), beyond it another, and another; what support lies under that one to bear its load? Beings of many kinds, colours and names: the account of them all has been written with an unceasing pen. Few have the skill to write this account; if it were written, how vast the account would be! How great is (God's) power, how beautiful his form! How great is his giving! Who can know its measure? With a single word he spread out the creation, and from it hundreds of thousands of rivers came to be. What power have I to voice a reflection (on your creation)? I am not worthy to be offered as a sacrifice (to you) even once. Whatever pleases you, that alone is a good deed. You abide for ever, safe and whole, O Formless Lord. ॥16॥

Panch here is not the number five: it is the word for the respected leaders of a community, and it means those who have listened and accepted, of whom Pauris 8 to 15 speak. Panche, with -e, is the Panch and no other; Pancha, in the fourth line, is of the Panch. The Faridkot Teeka also reads the word through the number five: those who have the five virtues, or have conquered the five vices.
At the courts of kings: the Panch are honoured in the world as well as in God's court. The Faridkot Teeka reads it as the door of the King, God.
The one Guru alone: their attention is aimed at the Guru and his word. Some read the Guru here as God, the One.

An old Puranic belief has the earth held up by a white bull (dhaval, dhaul). The Guru answers that what holds the world is dharam, God's law, born of compassion; and if a bull held the earth, it would need an earth beneath it and another bull beneath that, without end (hor, with -u, is masculine: another bull). Some read the line as more worlds beyond this one.
Jini is by which, that is by dharam; suti, in a thread, is in its order. Some translations instead take santokh as patience, with which dharam keeps the earth in its order.
Kavau is a word, a command: the whole creation spread out from one command of God, and from it came countless rivers, which the commentaries take as the streams of life.

Kudrat in Gurbani is God's power and the creation in which it is seen. In the refrain the word kavan, feminine, goes with kudrat, so the line asks what power I have; others read it as how can I describe your Kudrat. These four lines also close Pauris 17 and 19, and the last three close Pauri 18.
To be varia is to be offered up as a sacrifice, waved round the beloved; the Guru counts himself too small to be such an offering even once.
p17: Countless (beings) chant, countless are devoted in love. Countless worship, countless endure the heat of austerities. Countless recite sacred books and the Vedas with their mouths. Countless yogis stay inwardly detached (from the world). Countless devotees reflect on (God's) virtues and wisdom. Countless are the truthful, countless the givers. Countless are the warriors who take (the weapons') steel on their faces. Countless are the silent sages who keep their loving attention fixed in an unbroken line. What power have I to voice a reflection (on your creation)? I am not worthy to be offered as a sacrifice (to you) even once. Whatever pleases you, that alone is a good deed. You abide for ever, safe and whole, O Formless Lord. ॥17॥
Pauris 17 to 19 open line after line with asankh, countless: the devout, then the wicked, then names, places and worlds, all within the creation that the refrain says cannot be told.
Tap tau is the heat of tapas, bodily hardship taken on for spiritual merit.
Sati here are the people of truth and right conduct (sat), not the burning of a widow.
Muh bhakh sar, eating steel on the face: warriors who take the blows of weapons facing the enemy.
Moni are sages under a vow of silence; liv lai tar, with loving attention held in one unbroken line, like a stretched string.
p18: Countless are the fools, deep in blind darkness. Countless are the thieves and those who live on what is not theirs. Countless impose their commands by force, and pass away. Countless cut-throats commit murder. Countless sinners commit sin and pass away. Countless liars keep wandering in falsehood. Countless of foul mind devour filth as their food. Countless slanderers load the burden (of slander) on their own heads. Lowly Nanak offers (this) reflection. I am not worthy to be offered as a sacrifice (to you) even once. Whatever pleases you, that alone is a good deed. You abide for ever, safe and whole, O Formless Lord. ॥18॥
Haramkhor is one who lives on what is forbidden (haram), on what belongs to others.
Amar here is the Persian amr, command, not immortal: they rule others by force and in the end leave the world.
Malechh in Gurbani is one of foul mind and conduct, not a people; mal, filth, is what is unfit to eat; bhakh and khahi are both verbs for eating, so together they mean they devour it.

Nanaku nichu: both words end in -u, so Nanak is the subject and lowly describes him; in humility the Guru puts this line in place of the refrain's first line. Another reading is Nanak tells the state of the lowly.
p19: Countless are the names, countless the places; beyond reach, beyond reach, are the countless worlds. Those who say even countless take a load upon their heads. Through letters the Naam (is spoken), through letters (God's) praise; through letters, knowledge, songs and delving into (his) virtues; through letters, the writing and speaking of language; through letters, the destiny on the forehead is told. But he who wrote these (letters) has (no writing) on his own head. As he commands, so do (beings) receive. As much as he has made, so much is his Naam; there is no place without the Naam. What power have I to voice a reflection (on your creation)? I am not worthy to be offered as a sacrifice (to you) even once. Whatever pleases you, that alone is a good deed. You abide for ever, safe and whole, O Formless Lord. ॥19॥
Even the word countless sets a measure on what has none; those who use it take a burden of error on their heads.
Akhari, through letters, that is through words: though no word is enough, the Naam, praise, knowledge, song, writing and speech, and even the reading of destiny, all go by way of letters.
Gun gah: gah is to search through deeply, so it is delving into virtues.
Sanjog is the destiny joined to each being, by tradition written on the forehead; the One who writes it has no such writing over him.
Nau, the Naam, here is God made manifest: all that he has made is his Naam, and no place is empty of it.
p20: When the hands, the feet and the body are covered in dirt, washing with water takes the dust away. When a garment is soiled with urine, one puts soap on it and washes it clean. When the intellect is filled with sins, it is washed clean only in love of the Naam. Virtuous and sinful are not mere words to be said: whatever deeds you keep doing, you carry them with you, written down; you yourself sow, and you yourself eat (what you have sown). Says Nanak, by God's Hukam you come and go. ॥20॥
In love of the Naam: the word is rang, which means both colour and love; the intellect is washed clean by being dyed in love of the Naam.
Mere words: aakhanu, ending in -u, is a noun (a word, a name), not the verb to say. Virtuous and sinful are not names one is given; one's own deeds make one so, as the next lines say.
Carried with you, written down: the record of one's deeds goes with the soul. The Faridkot Teeka takes Chitr and Gupt (see Pauri 27) to be the ones who write it.
Come and go: are born and die, again and again.
p21: Pilgrimage, austerity, compassion and alms given in charity: if anyone gains anything by them, it is honour the size of a sesame seed. One who has heard (the Naam), accepted it, and brought love for it into the mind has bathed, scrubbing himself clean, at the place of pilgrimage within. All virtues are yours, (O Lord); I have none. Unless virtues are brought into being (in me, by you), there can be no devotion. Hail to you! You yourself are Maya, the Word and Brahma; you are true and beautiful, and joy is ever in your mind. What was that time, what that hour, what the lunar day, what the weekday, what were the seasons and what the month, when the form (of the world) came into being? The pandits did not find the time, or it would be written in a Purana; the qazis did not find the hour, or they would have written it in the Quran. No yogi knows the lunar day or the weekday, and no one knows the season or the month. The Creator who fashions the creation, he himself alone knows. How can I speak of him, how praise him, how describe him, how know him? O Nanak, everyone tries to speak of him, each thinking himself wiser than the other. Great is the Master and great his glory; all that happens is his doing. O Nanak, if anyone claims to know (him) by his own wit, he finds no honour when he goes on (to God's court). ॥21॥
Alms given in charity: datu daanu, a gift (daan) given (datu). A sesame seed is the smallest of measures: honour gained by such deeds is the least there is.
Bathed: naau here is the verb to bathe, not the noun Name; mali is scrubbing well. The place of pilgrimage within is one's own inner self.
Unless virtues are brought into being: the words are without virtues made. The line before says that all virtues are God's, so the maker is God. Some read it as without practising virtues.

Hail: suasati is the Sanskrit svasti, a word of blessing and salutation; aathi is Maya, the world's wealth; barmaau is Brahma, the creator god. Maya, the Word and Brahma were held to be the powers that bring the world into being; the line says that God himself is each of them. The Faridkot Teeka reads it as a sequence: from God joined with Maya came the Word, and from it Brahma and all creation.
Suhaanu: beautiful; it is also taken as the Arabic subhan, glorious and pure.
Time and hour: the Guru uses the Indian word vela with the pandits and the Arabic waqt (vakhatu) with the qazis. Thiti is the lunar day of the Indian calendar, vaaru the day of the week.
Qazis: kaadi is the Arabic qazi, a judge learned in Islamic law; Gurbani often writes d for the Arabic z, as in nadar for nazar.
By his own wit: aapau is of himself, by his own understanding. Going on is going on to the hereafter, to God's court.
p22: Netherworlds below netherworlds, hundreds of thousands of them, and skies above skies: people have searched for their very ends and grown weary; the Vedas say this one thing. The Katebs speak of eighteen thousand (worlds); their origin is one source. If it could be counted, the count would be written; but in the counting, the counting itself comes to an end. O Nanak, he is called great; he himself knows himself. ॥22॥
Tradition counts seven netherworlds below the earth and seven skies above it; the Guru speaks of hundreds of thousands.
This one thing: ik vaat, one word. Our reading: the Vedas all say this, that seekers have searched for the ends and grown weary. Some read it as the Vedas themselves having searched and grown weary.

Katebs: the four scriptures of the Semitic faiths, the Torah, the Zabur (Psalms), the Injil (Gospel) and the Quran. Eighteen thousand worlds is a count of Islamic tradition. Asulu is the Arabic asl, origin; ik dhaatu, one source, the one Creator.

In the counting: lekhai is in the reckoning; the numbers give out before creation is counted. The Faridkot Teeka also reads it as: whatever can be counted perishes; others, as: the one who counts perishes before the count is done.
p23: Praising the Praiseworthy One, no one has gained so much understanding (as to know how great he is); rivers and streams fall into the ocean and are no longer known (apart from it). Kings and sultans with realms as vast as the ocean, and wealth and riches heaped like mountains, are not equal to an ant, if you, (O Lord), do not slip from that ant's mind. ॥23॥

The Praiseworthy One: saalaahee is read here as the one worthy of praise, and saalaahi as having praised. Others read saalaahee as the praisers: those who praise him have not gained this understanding.
No longer known: jaaniahi is passive; once they enter the ocean the rivers are not known apart from it. So those who praise God merge in him without measuring him.
Vast as the ocean: samund saah sultan are kings and sultans of oceans, rulers of realms as great as seas; giraha seti, with mountains, is wealth heaped like mountains.
If you do not slip: viisarahi is second person; in the last line the Guru turns to address God.
p24: There is no end to his praises, and no end is reached by telling them. There is no end to his creation, and no end to his giving. No end is reached by seeing, and no end by hearing. No end can be seen to the counsel in his mind. No end can be seen to the form he has made. No end can be seen to his near shore or his far shore. So many wail and plead to find his limits, but his limits cannot be found. This end no one knows. The more is said of him, the greater he proves to be. Great is the Master, and high his place. Higher than the high is his Name. If anyone were as great and as high as he, only he would know that High One. How great he is, he himself knows, he alone. O Nanak, the Gracious One gives (every) gift by his kindness. ॥24॥
By telling, by seeing, by hearing: the ending -i in kahani, deni, vekhani and sunani marks the act or the means (in telling, in giving, in seeing, in hearing).
Mantu: counsel, the purpose God holds in his mind (Sanskrit mantra in its sense of counsel).
Paaraavaaru: the far shore and the near shore (Sanskrit paara and avaara), as of a river or the sea.
Nadari karami: nadari is the one whose glance is grace (from the Persian nazar, sight); karami is by grace (karam, kindness). The Faridkot Teeka reads karami as according to their deeds.
p25: His grace is so great that it cannot be written down. He is the great Giver, without a sesame seed's worth of greed. So many warriors beyond reckoning beg from him; so many more (beg) whose number cannot even be thought out. So many wear themselves out in vices and are broken. So many take and take, and then deny it. So many fools only go on eating. So many suffer pain, hunger and constant blows. These too are your gifts, O Giver. Release from bondage is by (your) will alone; no one can tell of any other (way). If some fool presumes to speak (of another), he alone knows how many blows he takes on his face. He himself knows, and he himself gives. Many, many say this too. One on whom he bestows (the gift of) his praise and glory, O Nanak, is the king of kings. ॥25॥
Karamu here is grace (karam, kindness), as in Pauri 24, not deeds. Tamaai is greed (the Arabic tama).
Mukaru paahi: deny it, as one who has received a gift and then disowns it.
Bandi khalaasi: release (khalaas) from bondage (band). The Faridkot Teeka reads it as bondage and release alike, both of which come by God's will.
Khaaiku: a foolish talker, a babbler. Blows on the face are disgrace; the Faridkot Teeka takes them as the punishment of the hereafter.
Many, many: kei kei is many and many. Some read it as few, very few: few are those who say this.
p26: Priceless are his virtues, priceless the dealing in them. Priceless are those who deal in them, priceless the treasuries. Priceless are those who come (for them), priceless those who take (them) away. Priceless are those in his love, priceless those absorbed in him. Priceless is his law, priceless his court. Priceless are the scales, priceless the weight. Priceless is his bounty, priceless its mark. Priceless is his grace, priceless his command. He is priceless beyond all price; (his worth) cannot be told. Describing him over and over, their minds fixed on him, people have grown weary. The readings of the Vedas and the Puranas describe him. The learned describe him and give discourses. The Brahmas describe him, the Indras describe him. The gopis and Govind describe him. The Shivas describe him, the Siddhas describe him. So many Buddhas, made by him, describe him. The demons describe him, the gods describe him. Godlike men, sages and those who serve him describe him. So many describe him, and so many set about describing him. So many, having described him over and over, rise and depart. If you were to make as many more as you have made, even then they could not describe (you), however many they were. He becomes as great as he pleases. O Nanak, that True One himself knows (how great he is). If some loudmouth claims to describe him, he is written down as the greatest fool among fools. ॥26॥
The pauri speaks in the image of trade: God's virtues are the goods, those who deal in them the traders, and his treasuries the stores.
Amul and amulu: in the first four lines amul, without the final -u, goes with plural nouns; from the fifth line amulu, with -u, goes with singular ones.
Dharamu is God's law; diibaanu (diwan) his court; tulu the scales and paravaanu the weight by which deeds are weighed; niisaanu the mark of his favour; phuramaanu (farman) his decree.
Grown weary: rahe is have been left, have given up. Some read it as remain: speaking of him over and over, they stay absorbed in him.
Gopis and Govind: the cowherd women of Braj and Krishna (Govind).
Brahmas, Indras, Shivas: barame, ind and iisar are plural; there are many of each, as Pauri 35 also says.
Suri nar: men of godly nature; muni jan: sages; sev: servants, devotees.
Boluvigaaru: one whose speech is spoiled, a loudmouth. Siri gaavaaraa gaavaaru: the fool at the head of fools.
p27: What is that gate like, and what is that home like, where (you) sit and take care of all? The sounds of countless instruments of many kinds play there, and so many are those who play them. So many ragas, with their raginis, are sung there, and so many are the singers. Wind, water and fire sing of you; Dharam Raj (the judge of souls) sings of you at your door. Chitr and Gupt, who know how to write, sing of you; what they write, Dharam Raj weighs and judges. Shiva, Brahma and the goddesses sing of you, ever beautiful, adorned by you. The Indras, seated on their thrones, sing of you with the gods at your door. The Siddhas sing of you in samadhi (deep meditative absorption); the sadhus sing of you in contemplation. The celibates, the charitable and the contented sing of you; the mighty heroes sing of you. The pandits and the great rishis who read (the scriptures) sing of you, age after age, along with the Vedas. The enchanting women who charm the mind sing of you, in heaven, in the mortal world and in the netherworld. The jewels you have created sing of you, along with the sixty-eight places of pilgrimage. Warriors of great might and heroes sing of you; the four sources of life sing of you. The regions, the worlds and the universes, made and set in place by you, sing of you. They alone sing of you who please you, your devotees, steeped (in your love) and full of delight. So many others sing of you who do not come to my mind; what can Nanak consider? He, he alone, is ever true; the Master is true, and true is his glory. He is, and he will be; he does not depart, nor will he depart, he who made the creation. He who brought forth Maya of many colours, many kinds and many species watches over what he has made, having made it, as befits his greatness. Whatever pleases him, that he will do; no command can be given (to him). He is the King, the Emperor over kings; O Nanak, (our part is) to live in his will. ॥27॥
Ragas and raginis: in Indian music each raga has its raginis, here pari, its consorts.
Dharam Raj judges each soul by its deeds; Chitr and Gupt are, by tradition, the two recorders at his court who write down the deeds of every being.
Idaasani: ind and aasani, on Indra's throne.
Sati: those of satu, truth and giving; here the charitable.
Rakhisar: rikhi and iisar, the great rishis. Mach is the mortal world, between heaven and the netherworld.
The jewels: by tradition, the fourteen jewels that came out of the ocean when it was churned. The sixty-eight places of pilgrimage are the tiraths held most holy in India.
The four sources of life (khaani): birth from the egg, from the womb, from sweat and from the earth.
Khand, mandal, varbhand: regions (each earth), spheres (each sun with its worlds) and universes (brahmand).
Rasaale: abodes of rasa, delight; the devotees who savour God's love.
Does not depart: jaai na jaasi, he does not go and will not go. The Darpan reads jaai as is born: he is not born and will not die.
Patisaahibu: pati and sahibu, the master over kings.
p28: (O yogi,) make contentment your earrings, effort your begging bowl and pouch, and meditation (on God) your ash; let death (kept in mind) be your patched coat, a body kept untouched (by vice) your discipline, and faith your staff. To hold all beings your fellows is to belong to the Aaee Panth; when the mind is conquered, the world is conquered. Homage, homage to him alone, who is the beginning (of all), stainless, without beginning, beyond destruction, and of one and the same form in every age. ॥28॥
Pauris 28 to 31 speak to the yogi in his own terms: his earrings, begging bowl, pouch, ash, patched coat and staff are each given an inner meaning.
Munda: the large earrings the Nath yogis wear through the split cartilage of the ear; bibhuti, the ash they smear on the body; khintha, the patched coat; danda, the staff.

Saram is read here as effort, toil (Sanskrit shram), and patu as the bowl (Sanskrit patra): the singular ending of ਪਤੁ sets it apart from ਪਤਿ, honour. The Faridkot Teeka reads saram as modesty and pat as honour.
Kuari kaia, a maiden body, is one kept untouched by vice; jugat is the yogi's rule of life.
Aaee Panth: the order held highest among the twelve orders of the yogis; jamati, those of one company, fellows.
Aadesu: the greeting yogis give one another; here it is given to God alone. The two closing lines are repeated at the end of Pauris 29, 30 and 31.
Anil: without stain (nil, dark); it is also read as without colour, or as beyond counting. Anahat: not struck down, imperishable. Vesu: form, guise, the same word as a yogi's garb.
p29: Let knowledge be your food and compassion its steward, and let the sound that plays in every heart be your Naad; he himself is the Nath (Master), who holds all (creation) by its nose-string; riddhis and siddhis are relishes of another kind (that lead away from him). Union and separation, the two, run the work (of the world); by the reckoning (of deeds) the shares come (to each). Homage, homage to him alone, who is the beginning (of all), stainless, without beginning, beyond destruction, and of one and the same form in every age. ॥29॥
Bhugat: the food yogis share at their common meal; bhandaran, the woman who keeps the stores and serves them out.
Naad: the horn yogis blow, among other times at their meal; here it is the sound that plays within every being.
Nath: master, the title of the heads of the yogi orders. Nathi: held by a nose-string, as an ox is by its nose-rope, under his control.
Riddhi is wealth and glory; siddhi, the miraculous powers (eight are counted) that yogis seek by their practices. Avra sad: tastes of something other than him.
Sanjog and vijog: the powers of God's will that bring beings together and part them. Bhag: the shares, as portions are served out at the yogis' meal.
p30: The one Mother (Maya), by some means, gave birth, and three disciples came forth for all to see: one peoples the world, one keeps its stores, one holds court. As it pleases him (God), so he makes them go, as his command may be. He watches them, but they do not see him; this is a great wonder. Homage, homage to him alone, who is the beginning (of all), stainless, without beginning, beyond destruction, and of one and the same form in every age. ॥30॥

The first two lines give the Puranic account: from Maya are born Brahma, who peoples the world (sansari), Vishnu, who keeps its stores and feeds all (bhandari), and Shiva, who holds court and destroys (lae dibanu). The next line sets all three under God's will and order.
Tini means three here; parvanu, with its singular ending, does not agree with chele (disciples) and is read as an adverb: manifestly, for all to see.
p31: His seat and his storehouses are in every world. Whatever (he) put into them, he put in once and for all. Creating again and again, the Creator watches over (what he has made). O Nanak, true is the work of the True One. Homage, homage to him alone, who is the beginning (of all), stainless, without beginning, beyond destruction, and of one and the same form in every age. ॥31॥
Aasan: the seat a yogi keeps for his practice; bhandar, the stores of a yogi camp.
The storehouses were filled once and never run short. The Faridkot Teeka also reads the line as: whatever each being receives (by his deeds), he receives at one time.
Vekhai: watches over, takes care of. Sacha: the True One, God who abides for ever; his work is true and unfailing.
p32: Let one tongue become a hundred thousand, and the hundred thousand become two million; let the one Name of the Lord of the world be spoken a hundred thousand times with each. On this path are the steps to the Husband-Lord; climbing them, (the soul) becomes one (with him). Hearing talk of the sky, worms were moved to imitate (and rise to it). O Nanak, (he) is attained by (his) grace; false is the boast of the false. ॥32॥
Lakh: a hundred thousand; lakh vis, twenty lakh, two million. Gera: a round, one turn of repetition.
Jagdis: the Lord of the world. Pat: the Husband-Lord (Sanskrit pati); pavrian, the rungs of a ladder.
Hoi ikis: becoming one with him. Prof. Sahib Singh reads hoi as having become: the steps are climbed only by one who has become one with him, the self given up.
The worms that hear of the sky and want to rise to it picture one who copies talk of the high state; the next line says it is reached by grace.
Thees: a boast, an empty claim.
p33: There is no power (of ours) in speaking, no power in keeping silent. No power in asking, no power in giving. No power in living, no power in dying. No power in (gaining) rule and wealth, over which the mind makes its clamour. No power in (gaining) awareness, knowledge or reflection. No power in the way by which the world (of birth and death) falls away. He in whose hands the power is, it is he who makes (all) and watches over it. O Nanak, no one is high or low (of himself). ॥33॥
Jor: power, the strength to have one's own way. The endings of akhan-i, chup-ai, mangan-i and the rest mark the locative: in speaking, in silence, in asking.
Surti: awareness, the waking of the spirit; the Faridkot Teeka reads it as shruti, the Vedas.
Sansar here is the round of birth and death; chhutai, it falls away, ends.
Soi: that very one, God; kar vekhai, he makes and watches over.
The last line echoes Pauri 2 (ਹੁਕਮੀ ਉਤਮੁ ਨੀਚੁ): high and low are by his Hukam, not by anyone's own power.
p34: Nights, seasons, lunar days and days of the week, winds, waters, fires and the nether regions: amid all these, God set the earth in place and kept it as a dharamsal (a place for living by dharam). On it are beings of many ways of life and many colours. Their names are many and without end. Each is judged by his own deeds. True is God himself, and true is his court. There the Panch shine for all to see. By the grace of the Gracious One, the mark (of honour) falls upon them. There it is found out who is unripe and who is ripe. O Nanak, only on going there is this known. ॥34॥

Pauris 34 to 37 tell of five khands, realms or stages of the spirit: Dharam Khand, Gian Khand, Saram Khand, Karam Khand and Sach Khand. This pauri is Dharam Khand, the realm of duty, named at the start of Pauri 35.
Thitis are the lunar days, fifteen in each half of the month; vars are the seven days of the week.

Tisu vichi (amid that), in the singular, takes in the whole gathering named in the first two lines; within all of it the earth is set as a dharamsal, a place where dharam, right living, is to be practised.
Ke in jugati ke rang means many, as in ke loa (of many worlds) in Pauri 37: beings of many ways and many colours.

Panch: see Pauri 16. There the plural paravan calls them accepted; here paravanu, singular, does not agree with the plural Panch and tells how they shine: manifestly, for all to see, as in Pauri 30. Many read this line too as the accepted Panch.
Nadari is God, the One whose glance is grace; karami, with its sihari, is by grace. The nisanu is the mark of honour that this grace sets on them.
Kach pakai: unripeness and ripeness, as of a clay pot unbaked or baked. Whether a life was raw or ripe is seen only in God's court, not by the standing it had in the world.
p35: Such is the dharam of Dharam Khand (the realm of duty). Now tell of the working of Gian Khand (the realm of knowledge). There are so many winds, waters and fires, and so many Krishnas and Shivas. So many Brahmas are fashioned in the mould, of many forms, colours and guises. So many lands of action, so many Merus, so many Dhrus and their teachings. So many Indras, moons and suns, so many spheres and lands. So many Siddhas, Buddhas and Naths, so many guises of goddesses. So many gods, demons and sages, so many jewels and oceans. So many sources of life, so many tongues, so many emperors and kings. So many forms of attention, so many servants; O Nanak, there is no end, no end. ॥35॥
Dharam Khand is the realm of Pauri 34: there one learns that the earth is a place for right living and that each is judged by his deeds. Eho (just this) points back to that pauri.
In Gian Khand the mind comes to see creation as endless: everything named in this pauri exists in countless numbers.
Kan is Kanh, Krishna; Mahesh is Shiva; Brahma is the creator god of the Puranas. Each is one of countless such beings within God's creation.
Ghariahi, passive and plural, says that the Brahmas themselves are fashioned. Some read it as the Brahmas fashioning creation.
Karam bhumi, lands of action, are lands where deeds are done and bear their fruit. Meru is the golden mountain at the centre of the world in the Puranas.
Dhru (Dhruva) is the boy devotee who, taught by the sage Narad, won an unshaken place and became the pole star.
Siddhas and Naths: see Pauri 8. Budh is taken as the Buddhas, the enlightened ones; some read it as the wise.
Khani: the sources of life (see Pauri 27); bani: speech, the tongues that beings speak.
Surati is the plural of surat, attention held in meditation (ketia goes with feminine nouns, kete with masculine). Some read it as the Shrutis, the Vedas, and the servants as those who serve them.
p36: In Gian Khand, knowledge blazes in its might. There is the bliss of music, delights and wonders. The make of Saram Khand (the realm of effort) is beauty. There (the mind) is shaped in the mould, beautiful beyond compare. The things of that realm cannot be told. If anyone tries to tell them, he regrets it afterwards. There awareness and intellect are shaped, and understanding in the mind. There the understanding of the gods and the Siddhas is shaped. ॥36॥
Saram is effort, toil (Sanskrit shram): Saram Khand is the realm of effort, where the mind is remade by the labour of devotion. Some read it as the Persian sharm, modesty.
Bani here, and in Pauri 37, is taken as the make, the form a thing is fashioned in. Some read it as speech: the speech of that realm is beauty.
Nad binod kod: sounds of music, delights and wonders; some take kod as crores, millions (of joys).
Gharati ghariai is a goldsmith's word, to be shaped in a mould; Pauri 38 takes up the image of the goldsmith.
Sura sidha ki sudhi: the insight of the gods and of the Siddhas, the perfected yogis.
p37: The make of Karam Khand (the realm of grace) is power. There is no other there, none other (than God). There are warriors, heroes of great might. In them Ram (the all-pervading Lord) is present to the full. There they are woven through and through into (God's) glory. Their beauty cannot be described. They neither die nor are deceived, those in whose minds Ram dwells. There dwell devotees of many worlds. They rejoice; that True One is in their minds. In Sach Khand (the realm of truth) dwells the Formless One. Creating again and again, he watches over his creation and makes it glad with his gracious glance. There are regions, spheres and universes; if anyone tries to tell of them, there is no end, no end. There are worlds upon worlds and forms. As his Hukam is, so is their working. Reflecting on it, he watches over it and delights in it. O Nanak, to tell of this is as hard as iron. ॥37॥
Karam here is grace: in Karam Khand God's grace fills one with a strength that nothing else can move. Bani, the make: see Pauri 36.
Horu na koi horu: the doubled horu makes it absolute, none but God at all. The same doubling is in sito sita and ant na ant below.
Sito sita: sewn and stitched, woven through (from sina, to sew), doubled for emphasis. The Faridkot Teeka reads Sita, the consort of Ram: the Lord's glory is his Sita, cool (sito, sital) and bright.
Na marahi: they do not die the death of the spirit; na thage jahi: Maya cannot cheat them.
Ke loa: of many worlds (ke, many, as in Pauri 34).
Sach Khand is the realm of truth, where the Formless One dwells and the soul is one with him.
Nadari nihal: the glance that makes blissful; nihal is one who is full of joy.
Karara saru: saru is iron; to put Sach Khand into words is as hard as iron.
p38: Let continence be the workshop and patience the goldsmith, the intellect the anvil and knowledge the hammer, the fear (of God) the bellows and the heat of austerity the fire, love the crucible, and in it melt the nectar (of the Naam): in such a true mint the Shabad (the Word) is fashioned. This is the work of those on whom rest (God's) glance and grace. O Nanak, the Gracious One makes them blissful with his glance. ॥38॥

The pauri is the goldsmith's craft: the pahara is his workshop, the khala the leather bellows that blow up his fire, the bhanda the crucible in which metal is melted, and the taksal the mint where coins are struck.
Jat, continence, is holding the senses back from vice.
Vedu, singular here like the other qualities of the pauri, means knowledge, not the books of the Vedas.
Amrit is the nectar of the Naam, which gives life that does not die.
In this mint the Shabad is fashioned: a life shaped by these qualities bears the Guru's Word as a coin bears its stamp.
salok.close: Air is the Guru, water the father, and the earth the great mother. Day and night are the two nurses, the female and the male; the whole world plays (in their care). In (God's) presence, Dharam (Raj) reads out the good deeds and the bad. By their own deeds, some are near (God) and some far. Those who meditated on the Naam have gone, their toil accomplished. O Nanak, their faces are bright, and many (others) have been set free along with them. ॥1॥
Pavanu is air and also breath, life itself: as the Guru gives life to the soul, breath gives life to the body. Some take it as the air that carries the Guru's word.
Water is the father because all life springs from it; the earth is the great mother who bears and feeds all.
Dai is a woman who nurses a child, daia a man who minds it. The day is taken as the male nurse and the night as the female: by day the world plays at its work, by night it sleeps.
Dharam Raj is the judge of souls (see Pauri 27), who reads out the record of each one's deeds before God.
Masakati is hard labour (Persian mashaqqat); ghali is having put it in, so that it bears fruit.
Keti chhuti nali: many others are freed in their company.

mool: There is one God, Ik Oankar, the One who pervades all and is ever the same; his Name is Sat (the One who truly is); he is the Creator, the Being who dwells in all,
his form beyond time, unborn, self-existent,
jap: Jap: the bani to be recited with the mind on God.
salok.open: The True One was there in the beginning; the True One was there when the ages began.
The True One exists now as well, O Nanak, and the True One will be hereafter too. ॥1॥
p1: Purity (of mind) does not come from washing (the body), though I wash a hundred thousand times.
Silence (of mind) does not come from keeping silent, though I stay absorbed in an unbroken thread of attention.
While I live in craving, the hunger does not go, though I tie up the loads (of goods) of all the worlds.
Though I had thousands, even hundreds of thousands, of clever ways, not one would go along with me.
How, then, can one become Sachiar (one who is true), and how is the wall of falsehood to be broken?
O Nanak, by walking in the Hukam (God's order, his will) of the Lord whose will it is; this (way) is written along with (every being from the start). ॥1॥
p2: By the Hukam, forms come into being; the Hukam cannot be described.
By the Hukam, beings come into being; by the Hukam, glory is received.
By the Hukam, one is high and another low; by the Hukam, as it is written, sorrows and joys are received.
Some, by the Hukam, are blessed with grace; others, by the Hukam, are made to wander forever (through births and deaths).
Everyone is within the Hukam; no one is outside the Hukam.
O Nanak, if one understands the Hukam, then no one speaks in Haumai (ego). ॥2॥
p3: Someone sings of his might, if anyone has the might (to sing it).
Someone sings of his gifts, taking them as his sign.
Someone sings of his virtues and his beautiful glories.
Someone sings, through learning, of hard thought about him.
Someone sings that he makes the body and then turns it to dust.
Someone sings that he takes away lives and gives them again.
Someone sings that he seems far off, that he appears far away.
Someone sings that he watches (all), ever present, face to face.
The telling (of him) never runs short.
Millions upon millions have told of him, telling and telling again.
The Giver goes on giving, and those who take from him grow tired.
Through age after age, they go on eating (what he gives).
The Commander's Hukam drives the way (of the world).
O Nanak, the carefree (Lord) is ever in bloom. ॥3॥
p4: The Master is true, and true is his justice; his language is love, and he is without limit.
All of us ask and beg him to give and give, and the Giver bestows his gifts.
What, then, should we place before him, by which his court may be seen?
What words should we speak with our mouth, on hearing which he may give us his love?
In the Amrit vela (the hours of nectar before daybreak), (remember) the true Naam (the Name, God's presence remembered) and reflect on his greatness.
By his grace comes the robe (of honour); by his glance of grace, the door of liberation.
O Nanak, in this way it is known that the True One himself is everywhere. ॥4॥
p5: He cannot be installed, nor can he be made.
That stainless one, Niranjan, exists of himself alone.
Whoever has served him has won honour.
O Nanak, let us sing of him, the treasure of virtues.
Let us sing, let us listen, and keep love for him in the mind.
Whoever does so casts off sorrow and carries peace home.
Through the Guru comes the Naad, through the Guru comes the Veda; through the Guru, God is known to pervade all.
The Guru is Shiva, the Guru is Gorakh and Brahma, the Guru is mother Parvati.
Even if I come to know him, I cannot tell of him; he cannot be put into words.
O Guru, give me this one understanding:
all beings have one giver; may I never forget him. ॥5॥
p6: I would bathe at a tirath (a place of pilgrimage) if by that I pleased him; without pleasing him, what would I gain by bathing?
All the creation he has brought forth that I see: without his grace, what does anyone receive, what can anyone take?
Jewels, gems and rubies lie within one's own understanding, if one listens to a single teaching of the Guru.
O Guru, give me this one understanding:
all beings have one giver; may I never forget him. ॥6॥
p7: Even if a person's life spanned the four ages, or ten times more,
if they were known throughout the nine regions of the earth, and everyone walked with them,
if, having made a good name, they won praise and renown in the world,
yet if they do not come into his gracious sight, no one asks after them.
God makes such a one a worm among worms, holds them guilty and lays the blame on them.
O Nanak, God creates virtue in the virtueless, and gives virtue to the virtuous.
No one else like him comes to mind who could give the virtueless one any virtue. ॥7॥
p8: By listening, one rises to the station of the Siddhas, the Pirs, the gods and the Naths.
By listening, one comes to understand the earth, the bull Dhaul said to bear it, and the sky.
By listening, one comes to understand the continents, the worlds and the nether regions.
By listening, death cannot touch one.
O Nanak, the devotees are ever in bloom.
By listening, sorrow and sin are destroyed. ॥8॥
p9: By listening, one rises to the station of Shiva, Brahma and Indra.
By listening, even a wicked person utters the Lord's praises with his mouth.
By listening, one comes to know the way of yoga and the secrets of the body.
By listening, one comes to understand the Shastras, the Simritis and the Vedas.
O Nanak, the devotees are ever in bloom.
By listening, sorrow and sin are destroyed. ॥9॥
p10: By listening come generosity, contentment and knowledge of God.
By listening, one has the bath at the sixty-eight tiraths.
By listening, one receives the honour that scholars win by reading and reading.
By listening, the mind's attention settles in Sahaj (natural, unshaken poise).
O Nanak, the devotees are ever in bloom.
By listening, sorrow and sin are destroyed. ॥10॥
p11: By listening, one comes to fathom oceans of virtue.
By listening, one rises to the station of the Sheikhs, the Pirs and the kings.
By listening, the blind find the way.
By listening, the depth of the fathomless ocean is found.
O Nanak, the devotees are ever in bloom.
By listening, sorrow and sin are destroyed. ॥11॥
p12: The state of one who has accepted (the Naam) cannot be told.
If anyone tries to tell it, he regrets it afterwards.
There is no one to write it on paper with a pen;
people sit together and reflect on the one who has accepted.
So exalted is the immaculate Naam (of God);
(this is known) if someone accepts it and comes to know it in his own mind. ॥12॥
p13: By accepting (the Naam), awareness and understanding arise in the mind.
By accepting, one comes to know of all the worlds.
By accepting, one does not suffer blows on the face.
By accepting, one does not go with Jam (the messenger of Death).
So exalted is the immaculate Naam (of God);
(this is known) if someone accepts it and comes to know it in his own mind. ॥13॥
p14: By accepting (the Naam), no obstacle blocks one's way.
By accepting, one departs (from the world) with honour, known to all.
By accepting, one does not walk the many roads and paths (of the sects).
By accepting, one's bond is with dharam (righteousness).
So exalted is the immaculate Naam (of God);
(this is known) if someone accepts it and comes to know it in his own mind. ॥14॥
p15: By accepting (the Naam), people find the door of liberation.
By accepting, one gives his family, too, (God's) support.
By accepting, the Guru himself crosses over and carries the Sikhs across.
By accepting, O Nanak, they do not wander about begging.
So exalted is the immaculate Naam (of God);
(this is known) if someone accepts it and comes to know it in his own mind. ॥15॥
p16: The Panch (those who have listened and accepted the Naam) are approved, the Panch are foremost.
It is the Panch who receive honour in the Dargah (the Lord's court).
It is the Panch who shine at the courts of kings.
The Panch keep their attention on the one Guru alone.
If anyone speaks of (the creation) and reflects on it,
(even then) there is no counting the Creator's making.
The bull (that holds up the earth) is dharam, the son of compassion,
which in its order has firmly established contentment.
If anyone understands this, he becomes Sachiar.
How great a load is on the bull!
Beneath the earth there would be another (bull), beyond it another, and another;
what support lies under that one to bear its load?
Beings of many kinds, colours and names:
the account of them all has been written with an unceasing pen.
Few have the skill to write this account;
if it were written, how vast the account would be!
How great is (God's) power, how beautiful his form!
How great is his giving! Who can know its measure?
With a single word he spread out the creation,
and from it hundreds of thousands of rivers came to be.
What power have I to voice a reflection (on your creation)?
I am not worthy to be offered as a sacrifice (to you) even once.
Whatever pleases you, that alone is a good deed.
You abide for ever, safe and whole, O Formless Lord. ॥16॥
p17: Countless (beings) chant, countless are devoted in love.
Countless worship, countless endure the heat of austerities.
Countless recite sacred books and the Vedas with their mouths.
Countless yogis stay inwardly detached (from the world).
Countless devotees reflect on (God's) virtues and wisdom.
Countless are the truthful, countless the givers.
Countless are the warriors who take (the weapons') steel on their faces.
Countless are the silent sages who keep their loving attention fixed in an unbroken line.
What power have I to voice a reflection (on your creation)?
I am not worthy to be offered as a sacrifice (to you) even once.
Whatever pleases you, that alone is a good deed.
You abide for ever, safe and whole, O Formless Lord. ॥17॥
p18: Countless are the fools, deep in blind darkness.
Countless are the thieves and those who live on what is not theirs.
Countless impose their commands by force, and pass away.
Countless sinners commit sin and pass away.
Countless liars keep wandering in falsehood.
Countless of foul mind devour filth as their food.
Countless slanderers load the burden (of slander) on their own heads.
I am not worthy to be offered as a sacrifice (to you) even once.
Whatever pleases you, that alone is a good deed.
You abide for ever, safe and whole, O Formless Lord. ॥18॥
p19: Countless are the names, countless the places;
beyond reach, beyond reach, are the countless worlds.
Those who say even countless take a load upon their heads.
Through letters the Naam (is spoken), through letters (God's) praise;
through letters, knowledge, songs and delving into (his) virtues;
through letters, the writing and speaking of language;
through letters, the destiny on the forehead is told.
But he who wrote these (letters) has (no writing) on his own head.
As he commands, so do (beings) receive.
As much as he has made, so much is his Naam;
there is no place without the Naam.
What power have I to voice a reflection (on your creation)?
I am not worthy to be offered as a sacrifice (to you) even once.
Whatever pleases you, that alone is a good deed.
You abide for ever, safe and whole, O Formless Lord. ॥19॥
p20: When the hands, the feet and the body are covered in dirt,
washing with water takes the dust away.
When a garment is soiled with urine,
one puts soap on it and washes it clean.
When the intellect is filled with sins,
it is washed clean only in love of the Naam.
Virtuous and sinful are not mere words to be said:
whatever deeds you keep doing, you carry them with you, written down;
you yourself sow, and you yourself eat (what you have sown).
Says Nanak, by God's Hukam you come and go. ॥20॥
p21: Pilgrimage, austerity, compassion and alms given in charity:
if anyone gains anything by them, it is honour the size of a sesame seed.
One who has heard (the Naam), accepted it, and brought love for it into the mind
has bathed, scrubbing himself clean, at the place of pilgrimage within.
All virtues are yours, (O Lord); I have none.
Unless virtues are brought into being (in me, by you), there can be no devotion.
Hail to you! You yourself are Maya, the Word and Brahma;
you are true and beautiful, and joy is ever in your mind.
What was that time, what that hour, what the lunar day, what the weekday,
what were the seasons and what the month, when the form (of the world) came into being?
The pandits did not find the time, or it would be written in a Purana;
the qazis did not find the hour, or they would have written it in the Quran.
No yogi knows the lunar day or the weekday, and no one knows the season or the month.
The Creator who fashions the creation, he himself alone knows.
How can I speak of him, how praise him, how describe him, how know him?
O Nanak, everyone tries to speak of him, each thinking himself wiser than the other.
Great is the Master and great his glory; all that happens is his doing.
O Nanak, if anyone claims to know (him) by his own wit, he finds no honour when he goes on (to God's court). ॥21॥
p22: Netherworlds below netherworlds, hundreds of thousands of them, and skies above skies:
people have searched for their very ends and grown weary; the Vedas say this one thing.
The Katebs speak of eighteen thousand (worlds); their origin is one source.
If it could be counted, the count would be written; but in the counting, the counting itself comes to an end.
O Nanak, he is called great; he himself knows himself. ॥22॥
p23: Praising the Praiseworthy One, no one has gained so much understanding (as to know how great he is);
rivers and streams fall into the ocean and are no longer known (apart from it).
Kings and sultans with realms as vast as the ocean, and wealth and riches heaped like mountains,
are not equal to an ant, if you, (O Lord), do not slip from that ant's mind. ॥23॥
p24: There is no end to his praises, and no end is reached by telling them.
There is no end to his creation, and no end to his giving.
No end is reached by seeing, and no end by hearing.
No end can be seen to the counsel in his mind.
No end can be seen to the form he has made.
No end can be seen to his near shore or his far shore.
So many wail and plead to find his limits,
but his limits cannot be found.
This end no one knows.
The more is said of him, the greater he proves to be.
Great is the Master, and high his place.
Higher than the high is his Name.
If anyone were as great and as high as he,
only he would know that High One.
How great he is, he himself knows, he alone.
O Nanak, the Gracious One gives (every) gift by his kindness. ॥24॥
p25: His grace is so great that it cannot be written down.
He is the great Giver, without a sesame seed's worth of greed.
So many warriors beyond reckoning beg from him;
so many more (beg) whose number cannot even be thought out.
So many wear themselves out in vices and are broken.
So many take and take, and then deny it.
So many fools only go on eating.
So many suffer pain, hunger and constant blows.
These too are your gifts, O Giver.
Release from bondage is by (your) will alone;
no one can tell of any other (way).
If some fool presumes to speak (of another),
he alone knows how many blows he takes on his face.
He himself knows, and he himself gives.
Many, many say this too.
One on whom he bestows (the gift of) his praise and glory,
O Nanak, is the king of kings. ॥25॥
p26: Priceless are his virtues, priceless the dealing in them.
Priceless are those who deal in them, priceless the treasuries.
Priceless are those who come (for them), priceless those who take (them) away.
Priceless are those in his love, priceless those absorbed in him.
Priceless is his law, priceless his court.
Priceless are the scales, priceless the weight.
Priceless is his bounty, priceless its mark.
Priceless is his grace, priceless his command.
He is priceless beyond all price; (his worth) cannot be told.
Describing him over and over, their minds fixed on him, people have grown weary.
The readings of the Vedas and the Puranas describe him.
The learned describe him and give discourses.
The Brahmas describe him, the Indras describe him.
The gopis and Govind describe him.
The Shivas describe him, the Siddhas describe him.
So many Buddhas, made by him, describe him.
The demons describe him, the gods describe him.
Godlike men, sages and those who serve him describe him.
So many describe him, and so many set about describing him.
So many, having described him over and over, rise and depart.
If you were to make as many more as you have made,
even then they could not describe (you), however many they were.
He becomes as great as he pleases.
O Nanak, that True One himself knows (how great he is).
If some loudmouth claims to describe him,
he is written down as the greatest fool among fools. ॥26॥
p27: What is that gate like, and what is that home like, where (you) sit and take care of all?
The sounds of countless instruments of many kinds play there, and so many are those who play them.
So many ragas, with their raginis, are sung there, and so many are the singers.
Wind, water and fire sing of you; Dharam Raj (the judge of souls) sings of you at your door.
Chitr and Gupt, who know how to write, sing of you; what they write, Dharam Raj weighs and judges.
Shiva, Brahma and the goddesses sing of you, ever beautiful, adorned by you.
The Indras, seated on their thrones, sing of you with the gods at your door.
The Siddhas sing of you in samadhi (deep meditative absorption); the sadhus sing of you in contemplation.
The celibates, the charitable and the contented sing of you; the mighty heroes sing of you.
The pandits and the great rishis who read (the scriptures) sing of you, age after age, along with the Vedas.
The enchanting women who charm the mind sing of you, in heaven, in the mortal world and in the netherworld.
The jewels you have created sing of you, along with the sixty-eight places of pilgrimage.
Warriors of great might and heroes sing of you; the four sources of life sing of you.
The regions, the worlds and the universes, made and set in place by you, sing of you.
They alone sing of you who please you, your devotees, steeped (in your love) and full of delight.
So many others sing of you who do not come to my mind; what can Nanak consider?
He, he alone, is ever true; the Master is true, and true is his glory.
He is, and he will be; he does not depart, nor will he depart, he who made the creation.
He who brought forth Maya of many colours, many kinds and many species
watches over what he has made, having made it, as befits his greatness.
Whatever pleases him, that he will do; no command can be given (to him).
He is the King, the Emperor over kings; O Nanak, (our part is) to live in his will. ॥27॥
p28: (O yogi,) make contentment your earrings, effort your begging bowl and pouch, and meditation (on God) your ash;
let death (kept in mind) be your patched coat, a body kept untouched (by vice) your discipline, and faith your staff.
To hold all beings your fellows is to belong to the Aaee Panth; when the mind is conquered, the world is conquered.
who is the beginning (of all), stainless, without beginning, beyond destruction, and of one and the same form in every age. ॥28॥
p29: Let knowledge be your food and compassion its steward, and let the sound that plays in every heart be your Naad;
he himself is the Nath (Master), who holds all (creation) by its nose-string; riddhis and siddhis are relishes of another kind (that lead away from him).
Union and separation, the two, run the work (of the world); by the reckoning (of deeds) the shares come (to each).
who is the beginning (of all), stainless, without beginning, beyond destruction, and of one and the same form in every age. ॥29॥
p30: The one Mother (Maya), by some means, gave birth, and three disciples came forth for all to see:
one peoples the world, one keeps its stores, one holds court.
As it pleases him (God), so he makes them go, as his command may be.
He watches them, but they do not see him; this is a great wonder.
who is the beginning (of all), stainless, without beginning, beyond destruction, and of one and the same form in every age. ॥30॥
p31: His seat and his storehouses are in every world.
Whatever (he) put into them, he put in once and for all.
Creating again and again, the Creator watches over (what he has made).
O Nanak, true is the work of the True One.
who is the beginning (of all), stainless, without beginning, beyond destruction, and of one and the same form in every age. ॥31॥
p32: Let one tongue become a hundred thousand, and the hundred thousand become two million;
let the one Name of the Lord of the world be spoken a hundred thousand times with each.
On this path are the steps to the Husband-Lord; climbing them, (the soul) becomes one (with him).
Hearing talk of the sky, worms were moved to imitate (and rise to it).
O Nanak, (he) is attained by (his) grace; false is the boast of the false. ॥32॥
p33: There is no power (of ours) in speaking, no power in keeping silent.
No power in asking, no power in giving.
No power in living, no power in dying.
No power in (gaining) rule and wealth, over which the mind makes its clamour.
No power in (gaining) awareness, knowledge or reflection.
No power in the way by which the world (of birth and death) falls away.
He in whose hands the power is, it is he who makes (all) and watches over it.
O Nanak, no one is high or low (of himself). ॥33॥
p34: Nights, seasons, lunar days and days of the week,
winds, waters, fires and the nether regions:
amid all these, God set the earth in place and kept it as a dharamsal (a place for living by dharam).
On it are beings of many ways of life and many colours.
Their names are many and without end.
Each is judged by his own deeds.
True is God himself, and true is his court.
There the Panch shine for all to see.
By the grace of the Gracious One, the mark (of honour) falls upon them.
There it is found out who is unripe and who is ripe.
O Nanak, only on going there is this known. ॥34॥
p35: Such is the dharam of Dharam Khand (the realm of duty).
Now tell of the working of Gian Khand (the realm of knowledge).
There are so many winds, waters and fires, and so many Krishnas and Shivas.
So many Brahmas are fashioned in the mould, of many forms, colours and guises.
So many lands of action, so many Merus, so many Dhrus and their teachings.
So many Indras, moons and suns, so many spheres and lands.
So many Siddhas, Buddhas and Naths, so many guises of goddesses.
So many gods, demons and sages, so many jewels and oceans.
So many sources of life, so many tongues, so many emperors and kings.
So many forms of attention, so many servants; O Nanak, there is no end, no end. ॥35॥
p36: In Gian Khand, knowledge blazes in its might.
There is the bliss of music, delights and wonders.
The make of Saram Khand (the realm of effort) is beauty.
There (the mind) is shaped in the mould, beautiful beyond compare.
The things of that realm cannot be told.
If anyone tries to tell them, he regrets it afterwards.
There awareness and intellect are shaped, and understanding in the mind.
There the understanding of the gods and the Siddhas is shaped. ॥36॥
p37: The make of Karam Khand (the realm of grace) is power.
There is no other there, none other (than God).
There are warriors, heroes of great might.
In them Ram (the all-pervading Lord) is present to the full.
There they are woven through and through into (God's) glory.
Their beauty cannot be described.
They neither die nor are deceived,
those in whose minds Ram dwells.
There dwell devotees of many worlds.
They rejoice; that True One is in their minds.
In Sach Khand (the realm of truth) dwells the Formless One.
Creating again and again, he watches over his creation and makes it glad with his gracious glance.
There are regions, spheres and universes;
if anyone tries to tell of them, there is no end, no end.
There are worlds upon worlds and forms.
As his Hukam is, so is their working.
Reflecting on it, he watches over it and delights in it.
O Nanak, to tell of this is as hard as iron. ॥37॥
p38: Let continence be the workshop and patience the goldsmith,
the intellect the anvil and knowledge the hammer,
the fear (of God) the bellows and the heat of austerity the fire,
love the crucible, and in it melt the nectar (of the Naam):
in such a true mint the Shabad (the Word) is fashioned.
This is the work of those on whom rest (God's) glance and grace.
O Nanak, the Gracious One makes them blissful with his glance. ॥38॥
salok.close: Air is the Guru, water the father, and the earth the great mother.
Day and night are the two nurses, the female and the male; the whole world plays (in their care).
In (God's) presence, Dharam (Raj) reads out the good deeds and the bad.
By their own deeds, some are near (God) and some far.
Those who meditated on the Naam have gone, their toil accomplished.
O Nanak, their faces are bright, and many (others) have been set free along with them. ॥1॥
